 KLAS Las Vegas Follow School loan repayments emerge as Nevada campaign issue
 Joshua Peguero Sun, October 25, 2026 at 6:20 PM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. LAS VEGAS (KLAS) -- As the price of higher education climbs, so do the number of students taking out loans and the amount they borrow.
 During her visit to North Las Vegas last week, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said it's a cycle that needs to shift, and she blames universities.
  Education secretary visits CSN, highlights its workforce programs  
 "[They're] treating students like blank checks too often to justify endless tuition and fee increases," McMahon said.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Sec. McMahon made those comments last Wednesday at the College of Southern Nevada in North Las Vegas. Federal data showed that 28% of CSN students who began making loan payments in 2020 are now behind. It's the highest out of any public college or university in Nevada.
  Education Secretary Linda McMahon testifies before Congress  
 McMahon has overseen the dismantling of the education department at the urging of President Donald Trump. She ended the pandemic-era pause on school loan payments, which has become a campaign issue.
 "What we've been trying to do is to unravel, literally, what was a mess from the Biden Administration," McMahon said. "With all of the talk of all loans being forgiven and all of that, people stopped paying. They got confused about what they needed to do."
 Advertisement Advertisement  Linda McMahon confirmed as Trump's Education secretary  
 The U.S. Department of Treasury now manages the federal student loan portfolio.
 "Get people out of default, that's kind of the first tranche that the Department of Treasury is doing," McMahon said.
 Nevada is among the states with the highest student loan default rates. Federal data showed 93,000 Nevadans are in default as of this year in March, owing more than $2 billion.
 "There are right now like 7 or 8 different programs," McMahon said. "You can get back into your old program, as long as you start paying again."
 One that isn't available is the Biden-era SAVE program. It was considered the most affordable school loan repayment plan. A federal court struck down SAVE earlier this year.
 Advertisement Advertisement "In 2028, the program that will be available is two payment systems. That can be tiered relative to income, but it's primarily two payment systems, and hopefully, by then, we'll have everybody back on track, understanding how their payments work," McMahon said.
 According to the Treasury Department, the agency is managing $1.7 trillion of student loan debt with fewer than half of borrowers current in their repayment. Almost a quarter are in default.
 Battle Born Progress, a progressive action group, issued a statement regarding reports that the Department of Education plans to garnish the wages of borrowers in default.
 "Think what that means for a teacher, a nurse, or a casino worker already stretched thin by rent, groceries, and health care costs. Losing a piece of every paycheck isn't a minor inconvenience. It means missed rent and deeper debt," Shelbie Swartz, the executive director of Battle Born Progress said.
